title: The Village and the Spider Hole: al-Awja, the Palaces, and the Road Back to al-Awja
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Al-Awja, the birth in the mud-brick village
stops.campa: Thirteen kilometres south of Tikrit, on the west bank of the Tigris, a landless peasant family in the village of al-Awja receives a son. The father, Hussein Abd al-Majid, is already gone; the sources cannot decide whether he died or simply walked away, and no one records which. The mother, Subha, names the boy Saddam, one who confronts. There is no birth certificate, no photograph, no house that survives to be pointed at. The village is a scatter of mud brick above a river that has carried empires past this bank for four thousand years, and it will be the first and the last address of his life.
suggested_refs: The village of al-Awja, 13 km south of Tikrit on the west bank of the Tigris

stops.name: Al-Awja, the stepfather's house
stops.campa: Subha remarries. Her new husband, Ibrahim al-Hassan, is remembered in the exile biographies as a man who beat the boy and sent him out to steal chickens and sheep; his relatives dispute the severity, and no document exists to settle it either way. Between the disappearance of the father and this second household the accounts also place a suicide attempt by the mother and the death of an older brother, all of it reported, none of it filed. The official biographies published after 1968 keep the poverty and the missing father and say nothing about the beatings or the thefts.
suggested_refs: Said K. Aburish, Saddam Hussein: The Politics of Revenge (2000)
Con Coughlin, Saddam: His Rise and Fall (2002)

stops.name: Baghdad, the house of Khairallah Talfah
stops.campa: At about ten he runs from the stepfather to his maternal uncle Khairallah Talfah, a cashiered army officer and Arab nationalist who becomes the only father he will acknowledge. Wikipedia puts the uncle's house in Baghdad; Aburish and Coughlin put the first refuge at Tikrit with the capital coming later, and the two versions are not reconciled. The city he enters is the city of Junayd al-Baghdadi, who taught and died here, and of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, whose tomb at Bab al-Sheikh has drawn pilgrims for eight hundred years. The boy is not brought to see either.
suggested_refs: The household of Khairallah Talfah, guardian and later governor of Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, Karkh secondary school and the party
stops.campa: He finishes primary school at Tikrit late, then enrols at Karkh secondary school in the western half of Baghdad, where Arab nationalist student politics is the weather in every classroom. Talfah's house supplies the doctrine and the grievances, the school supplies the crowd. In 1957, at twenty, he joins the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party, drawn to a programme that promises one Arab nation, no monarchy, and no British hand on the oil. He will later begin law study and abandon it for the party. The exact school building is not identified in the sources; the pin marks the district.
suggested_refs: Karkh secondary school, Baghdad, and the Ba'ath student cells of the mid-1950s

stops.name: Tikrit, the marriage to Sajida Talfah
stops.campa: He marries Sajida Khairallah Talfah, his first cousin and the daughter of the uncle who raised him, in a match arranged when both were children. Five children will follow across fourteen years: Uday in 1964, Qusay in 1966, Raghad in 1968, Rana in 1969, Hala in 1972. The marriage binds him permanently into the Tikriti clan network that will staff the security services, the Republican Guard, and half the cabinet of the state he has not yet imagined. Several accounts date this wedding to 1963, after the Cairo exile; the sources that name the year give 1958, before the gun on Rashid Street.
suggested_refs: The Talfah family and the Tikriti clan network of the later Ba'athist state

segments.name: Rashid Street and the Cairo Years

stops.name: Baghdad, the fall of the monarchy
stops.campa: Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim's Free Officers overthrow the Hashemite monarchy; the king and the crown prince are killed, the prime minister is torn apart in the street, and the British-aligned order in Iraq ends in a morning. The Ba'ath Party celebrates and then turns, within a year, against the man who made the revolution: Qasim leans on the Iraqi Communist Party, refuses union with Nasser's Egypt, and becomes in Ba'athist eyes the obstacle rather than the instrument. The party begins looking for young men willing to shoot him. Saddam is twenty-one.
suggested_refs: The 14 July Revolution and the killing of Faisal II

stops.name: Rashid Street, the ambush of Qasim
stops.campa: A Ba'athist team opens fire on Qasim's car on Rashid Street, the long colonnaded artery through old Baghdad. The prime minister is hit and survives; his driver is killed; the gunmen scatter. Saddam is one of them, and is himself wounded. What he did in that minute is told two ways. The state will publish it as his ordeal; Karsh and Rautsi read the heroic frame, the leg wound dug out with a razor and all, as mythology assembled after 1968 by a government with a printing press.
suggested_refs: Rashid Street, Baghdad, site of the 7 October 1959 attempt on Abd al-Karim Qasim

stops.name: Tikrit, the flight toward the border
stops.campa: Wounded, he goes north overland through Tikrit and out toward the Syrian frontier, then on through Damascus. The escape as it will be told in schoolbooks and in a feature film has him swimming the Tigris in the dark with a knife between his teeth; historians treat the river crossing as embellishment added later. What the record holds is a young man on back roads with a hole in his leg and a death sentence in absentia behind him. He is twenty-two and will not see Iraq again for three years.
suggested_refs: The overland escape route from Baghdad through Tikrit to the Syrian border

stops.name: Cairo, the exile and the law school
stops.campa: He arrives in Nasser's Cairo by early 1960 and stays three years under Egyptian protection, on a stipend, among the exiled Iraqi Ba'athists who fill the coffeehouses arguing about a revolution none of them are currently in. He enrols at Cairo law school and does not finish. The address given in the sources, an apartment near Ain Shams, is an approximation and not a documented one. He leaves Cairo without the degree. The man running the city is a colonel who took a country and nationalized a canal, and whose voice carries Arab nationalism on every radio from Rabat to Basra.
suggested_refs: The Iraqi Ba'athist exile community in Cairo, 1960-1963

stops.name: Baghdad, the Ramadan Revolution and the return
stops.campa: The Ba'ath and its army allies take Baghdad; Qasim is tried in a room and shot within hours, and his body is shown on television. Saddam comes home within weeks and is given a place in the party's regional command. He does not go to a ministry. He goes into the internal security and interrogation apparatus, the machinery that decides who is questioned and for how long, and he learns it from the inside in the nine months before the Ba'ath loses power again in November. He will keep a hand on that apparatus for the next forty years.
suggested_refs: The Ramadan Revolution of February 1963 and the first Ba'athist government

stops.name: Qasr al-Nihayah, the Palace of the End
stops.campa: Arrested in October 1964 under the successor regime, he spends most of two years in custody. Several accounts place part of the imprisonment at the Qasr al-Nihayah, the Palace of the End, the old royal residence where the last king's family was killed in 1958 and which has since become a security house; other accounts put the main confinement elsewhere in Baghdad, and the sources do not agree. He escapes in 1966. State media will retell the escape as a feat of nerve, and every detail of that telling comes from the state rather than from a document.
suggested_refs: Qasr al-Nihayah, Baghdad, royal palace turned Ba'athist security house

stops.name: Republican Palace, the 17 July Revolution
stops.campa: The Ba'ath takes power a second time, against President Abd al-Rahman Arif, and this time keeps it for thirty-five years. The coup is bloodless: Arif is put on a plane to London. Ahmad Hassan al-Bakr, secretary-general of the party and a kinsman from Tikrit, becomes president and makes Saddam his deputy and deputy chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council. Saddam had been appointed deputy secretary-general of the party in 1966, two years earlier. The published account in which he personally commands the tank that storms the palace is his own, told later, and fits nothing else about the day.
suggested_refs: The 17 July Revolution and the Ba'athist seizure of the Republican Palace

stops.name: Baghdad, the Revolutionary Command Council
stops.campa: As vice chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council he takes the security services for his own portfolio. Over a decade he builds them out from party militia into an interlocking apparatus of intelligence, counter-intelligence, party police, and informers, staffed heavily from Tikrit and from his own clan, answering to him and not to the president. Al-Bakr is the face of the state. Saddam is the file on every man in it. He is thirty-two when he begins, and he builds no second base of power because he does not need one.
suggested_refs: The Revolutionary Command Council and the Ba'athist security services, 1969-1979

stops.name: Baghdad, the nationalization of the oil
stops.campa: He oversees the nationalization of the Iraq Petroleum Company, taking the fields out of the hands of the Anglo-American consortium that has held them since the mandate. Within eighteen months the price of oil quadruples, and the revenue of the Iraqi state multiplies past anything its planners have ever costed. The money buys literacy campaigns, hospitals, electrification of the villages, free universities, and a decade in which Iraq's social indicators lead the Arab world. It also buys the security services, the army, and every palace that follows.
suggested_refs: The nationalization of the Iraq Petroleum Company, June 1972

stops.name: Algiers, the accord with the Shah
stops.campa: At an OPEC summit in Algiers he signs with Mohammad Reza Shah an agreement moving the Shatt al-Arab boundary to the deepest channel, conceding half the waterway to Iran, in exchange for Iran cutting off the arms and sanctuary keeping the Kurdish rebellion alive. The rebellion collapses within weeks. He gets his northern war ended and pays for it in river. He will call the concession a humiliation for the rest of his life, and five years later he will tear the document up on television as the justification for invading the country he signed it with.
suggested_refs: The Algiers Agreement of 6 March 1975 on the Shatt al-Arab boundary

stops.name: Paris, the reactor negotiations
stops.campa: He travels to France to buy a nuclear research reactor and is received by Prime Minister Jacques Chirac, who calls him a personal friend and shows him around Provence. The reactor, Osirak, is sold to Iraq with French fuel and French technicians. Israeli aircraft destroy it on the ground in June 1981. European and American governments go on selling to him for another fifteen years, and afterwards describe him as having been recognizable for what he was the entire time.
suggested_refs: The Osirak reactor contract and the Chirac visit of 1975

stops.name: Republican Palace, sworn in as president
stops.campa: Al-Bakr resigns, citing ill health. The health is real and the resignation is not voluntary; Saddam has spent eleven years making the presidency a title that describes what he already does. He takes the office, the chairmanship of the Revolutionary Command Council, and the command of the armed forces in a single afternoon. He has been promoted general three years earlier, having never served a day in the army. He is forty-two years old and there is no longer any person in Iraq positioned above him.
suggested_refs: The resignation of Ahmad Hassan al-Bakr, 16 July 1979

stops.name: Al-Khuld Hall, the reading of the names
stops.campa: Six days after taking the presidency he convenes the party leadership at Al-Khuld Hall and has the session filmed. A confession of a Syrian plot is read out. Then Saddam, smoking a cigar at the podium, begins reading names from a list, and one by one sixty-eight men are led out of the room by guards while the survivors chant their loyalty. Twenty-two are shot, and members of the remaining leadership are handed rifles and made to serve on the firing squads. Copies of the film are distributed to Ba'ath branches across the country. The point of the film is that it exists.
suggested_refs: The filmed Ba'ath Party purge at Al-Khuld Hall, 22 July 1979
sources: BBC and CNN retrospectives on the purge film

stops.name: Shatt al-Arab, the invasion of Iran
stops.campa: Iraqi columns cross the Shatt al-Arab and the Iranian border on a six-hundred-kilometre front. The revolution in Tehran has shot its own generals and grounded its air force, and the calculation in Baghdad is a short war for the waterway and the Arab-populated oil province beyond it. The chain running into this morning is long: Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalized Iran's oil and was removed in 1953, the Shah was restored, the Shah fell in 1979, and Khomeini took his place. Saddam invades the country the 1953 coup produced. The short war lasts eight years.
suggested_refs: The Iraqi invasion of Iran, 22 September 1980, and the Shatt al-Arab crossings

stops.name: Dujail, the reprisal
stops.campa: Gunmen fire on the presidential motorcade passing through Dujail, a Shia farming town north of Baghdad. Nobody in the convoy is hurt. The response takes the town apart: helicopters strafe the orchards, the date palms are bulldozed, hundreds are taken away, and one hundred and forty-eight men and boys are put to death, some after years in detention. The paperwork survives, signed. Of everything done in twenty-four years of rule this is the file that will be complete enough to try, and it is the one he will be hanged for.
suggested_refs: The Dujail reprisal of July 1982 and its surviving execution orders

stops.name: Basra, the southern front and the gas
stops.campa: The war settles into the marshes and the flooded fields outside Basra and stops moving, a First World War fought with Migs: trench lines, barbed wire, human-wave assaults by Iranian teenagers, and from 1983 mustard gas and then nerve agent fired by Iraqi artillery into the massed infantry. He visits the front repeatedly, in uniform, filmed. Six centuries earlier al-Qushayri's caravan crossed from Iran into Iraq at Hulwan in the Zagros, calling it the boundary between the two lands; the trench line runs near the same ground.
suggested_refs: The Basra front and the Iraqi chemical warfare programme, 1983-1988

stops.name: Babylon, the bricks with his name in them
stops.campa: While the front stands still he rebuilds Babylon. New walls rise on the old foundations, and the bricks are stamped in the manner of the king who built the first ones: this was constructed by Saddam Hussein, son of Nebuchadnezzar, to glorify Iraq. Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem and carried a nation into exile from this ground; Alexander died here, thirty-two years old, having taken everything between Macedon and the Indus. The new brick is poor quality and sits badly on the old. Archaeologists will spend decades trying to get it off.
suggested_refs: The 1980s reconstruction of Babylon and its inscribed bricks

stops.name: Halabja, the gas on the town
stops.campa: Iraqi aircraft bomb the Kurdish town of Halabja with mustard gas and nerve agent over several hours. Between three thousand two hundred and five thousand civilians die, most of them in their houses and in the streets they ran into; the photographs of families lying where they fell go around the world within days. It is the deadliest chemical attack on a civilian population in modern history. Ali Hassan al-Majid, his cousin, directs the Anfal campaign of which Halabja is one day. Whether the order for this town came from Saddam personally is still argued.
suggested_refs: Human Rights Watch, Genocide in Iraq: The Anfal Campaign Against the Kurds (1993)

stops.name: The Iran-Iraq border, the ceasefire
stops.campa: A United Nations ceasefire ends the war on the line it started from. Eight years, roughly a million dead between the two countries, no territory changed hands, and the Shatt al-Arab boundary is exactly where the Algiers Agreement he tore up had put it. Iraq owes something near eighty billion dollars, much of it to Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. He declares the outcome the Qadisiyyah of Saddam, a second victory of Arabs over Persians thirteen centuries after the first, and builds an arch of crossed swords in Baghdad to say so.
suggested_refs: The Victory Arch (Swords of Qadisiyah), Baghdad, opened 8 August 1989

segments.name: Kuwait and the Mother of All Battles

stops.name: Kuwait City, the Seif Palace
stops.campa: Republican Guard divisions cross the border before dawn and are in Kuwait City by morning; the Emir's Seif Palace on the waterfront is taken within hours and the Emir is over the Saudi border. The stated grievances are overproduction of oil against the OPEC quota and slant-drilling into the Rumaila field; the unstated one is the war debt owed to the country now being annexed. Days later Kuwait is declared the nineteenth province of Iraq. Within a week American divisions begin landing in Saudi Arabia and thirty-four countries begin assembling against him.
suggested_refs: The Seif Palace, Kuwait City, seized 2 August 1990

stops.name: Baghdad, the takbir written on the flag
stops.campa: Four days before the bombing starts, the words Allahu Akbar are added between the three stars of the Iraqi flag, written in a hand the state says is his own. The Ba'ath Party was founded secular, by a Christian, on the proposition that the Arab nation precedes the Muslim one. The coalition massing in the desert is led by the United States and hosted by the guardians of Mecca, and the war about to begin needs to be a war of faith. The flag changes in a week. It will keep the takbir for twenty-six years, outliving him by eleven.
suggested_refs: The addition of the takbir to the flag of Iraq, January 1991

stops.name: Al-Amiriyah, the shelter
stops.campa: Two laser-guided bombs cut through the roof of a civil defence shelter in the Amiriyah district of Baghdad in the small hours. More than four hundred people are inside, mostly women and children sleeping through the air campaign; the steam from the ruptured pipes kills those the blast does not. The United States maintains it had intelligence identifying the structure as a military command bunker. Iraqi state television takes the world's press through it that morning. The building is left standing afterwards, unrepaired, and preserved as a memorial.
suggested_refs: The Amiriyah shelter, Baghdad, preserved after the bombing of 13 February 1991

stops.name: Safwan, the tent at the airfield
stops.campa: In a tent at Safwan airfield, just inside Iraq near the Kuwaiti border, Norman Schwarzkopf receives Lieutenant General Sultan Hashim Ahmad and sets out the ceasefire terms. Saddam is not there and sends no representative of his own rank. The Iraqi delegation asks permission to fly helicopters inside Iraq, on the grounds that the roads and bridges are destroyed, and is granted it. Those helicopters will be over Najaf and Karbala within a fortnight. The army is expelled from Kuwait; the man who sent it in is still in the Republican Palace.
suggested_refs: The Safwan ceasefire talks, 3 March 1991

stops.name: Najaf, the shrine under shellfire
stops.campa: The south rises, and then the north. Republican Guard armour retakes the Shia cities one by one, and at Najaf the shelling damages the precinct around the shrine of Imam Ali, the holiest ground in Shia Islam and the burial place of the Prophet's cousin. Tanks entering Karbala carry banners reading no Shia after today. Tens of thousands are killed across both risings; two million Kurds run for the Turkish and Iranian mountains in March snow. The coalition, three weeks past its victory, watches from the air and does not intervene.
suggested_refs: The Imam Ali Shrine, Najaf, damaged in the suppression of the March 1991 uprising

stops.name: Baghdad, the Faith Campaign
stops.campa: He announces al-Hamla al-Imaniya, the Faith Campaign. Quran study becomes compulsory in schools and in the party, alcohol is restricted, nightclubs close, mosques are built by the hundred, and the punishments of amputation and branding enter the penal code. A secular Arab nationalist party begins issuing religious credentials. The country under it is starving: the sanctions regime has collapsed the currency, the hospitals are out of everything, and infant mortality is climbing. Piety costs the treasury nothing, and the treasury has nothing.
suggested_refs: The Faith Campaign (al-Hamla al-Imaniya), announced June 1993

stops.name: Radwaniyah, the Al-Faw Palace
stops.campa: On an artificial lake at Radwaniyah, outside Baghdad, he raises the Al-Faw Palace, named for the peninsula retaken from Iran in 1988: marble halls, chandeliers, a hundred rooms, an island reached by causeways. It is one of dozens built during the sanctions decade while the ration card shrinks. The financing runs through the oil-for-food arrangements and the same grey banking channels that carried Iran-Contra money and Manuel Noriega's accounts a decade earlier at BCCI, the bank the regulators shut in 1991. American generals will run the occupation from these rooms.
suggested_refs: Al-Faw Palace, Radwaniyah, later the MNF-I headquarters at Camp Victory

stops.name: Baghdad, the mosque begun on his birthday
stops.campa: Ground is broken for the Umm al-Ma'arik Mosque, the Mother of All Battles, on his sixty-first birthday. Four inner minarets stand thirty-seven metres for the year of his birth and are shaped like the barrels of Kalashnikovs; four outer minarets stand forty-three metres for the forty-three days of the 1991 war and are shaped like Scud missiles. Inside, on display, is a Quran said to be written out in his own blood, six hundred pages of it, given over two years by a nurse keeping count. The building is finished in 2001.
suggested_refs: The Umm al-Qura (Umm al-Ma'arik) Mosque, Baghdad, and the Blood Quran

stops.name: Baghdad, Zabibah and the King
stops.campa: A novel appears in Iraq, published anonymously, universally understood to be his: a king learns to love his people through a peasant woman named Zabibah, who is raped on the seventeenth of January, the night the bombing began in 1991. It is made into a twenty-part television series and a musical at the National Theatre, and given to visiting delegations as a gift. The CIA reads it and concludes he did not write it. In four years an FBI agent will sit across a table and read passages of it back to him, watching what he does with his face.
suggested_refs: Zabibah and the King (Baghdad, 2000; English translation 2004)
sources: FBI Interview Session 1, 7 February 2004, National Security Archive EBB No. 279

stops.name: Baghdad, the bunkers under the invasion
stops.campa: The coalition invades on the stated grounds of weapons of mass destruction that the inspectors have not found and that do not exist. He directs the defence from command bunkers under Baghdad and appears on state television in uniform and glasses, reading statements, while his information minister tells the press there are no American tanks in the capital with American tanks audible behind him. Three weeks is all it takes. On the ninth of April he leaves the last bunker and goes into the country with his sons and a few cars.
suggested_refs: The 2003 invasion of Iraq and the fall of Baghdad, 9 April 2003

stops.name: Firdos Square, the statue comes down
stops.campa: A Marine recovery vehicle puts a chain around the neck of the bronze in Firdos Square and pulls it off its plinth, and the image runs on every network on earth as the end of the regime. The square is outside the hotel where the international press is billeted. Later analysis of the wide shots finds the crowd small, a few dozen where the framing suggested thousands, and whether the toppling was staged or spontaneous is still argued by the people who were standing there. The statue had been raised the previous April, for his sixty-fifth birthday.
suggested_refs: The Firdos Square statue, raised April 2002, toppled 9 April 2003
sources: Los Angeles Times analysis of the crowd footage (2004)

stops.name: Mosul, the house where the sons die
stops.campa: An informant gives up a house in Mosul. Uday and Qusay hold it for four hours against American infantry and helicopters, with Qusay's fourteen-year-old son Mustafa firing from an upstairs room and still firing after both his father and his uncle are dead. The bodies are identified by dental records, reconstructed by morticians, and photographed for release, because nobody in Iraq will otherwise believe it. Uday had run the Fedayeen and the Olympic Committee and its prison. The line of succession he spent thirty years assembling ends in one afternoon.
suggested_refs: The Mosul firefight of 22 July 2003 and the deaths of Uday and Qusay Hussein

stops.name: Ad-Dawr, the spider hole
stops.campa: Eight months a fugitive, moving between farmhouses and safe rooms in the country south of Tikrit, sheltered by men from his own tribe. On a farm outside Ad-Dawr, soldiers pull back a rug and a slab of styrofoam and find a hole in the ground a metre wide with an air pipe and a fan. He comes out with a beard to his chest, two AK-47s and seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars in the hut above, and does not fire. Al-Awja, where he was born, is thirteen kilometres north across the river.
suggested_refs: The capture site at Ad-Dawr, Operation Red Dawn, 13 December 2003

stops.name: Baghdad International Airport, the examination
stops.campa: He is flown by helicopter to the Tikrit mission support site and on to the airport the same night. A military doctor in latex gloves checks his scalp for lice, shines a light in his eyes, and presses a wooden spatula on his tongue while a camera runs; the footage is released the following day and played on a loop in every capital. The airport he lands at is named for him. The palace he built at Radwaniyah, four kilometres away, is now the headquarters of the army holding him.
suggested_refs: The medical examination footage released 14 December 2003

stops.name: Camp Cropper, the sessions with the FBI
stops.campa: Held near the airport, isolated from the other high-value detainees, he is interviewed across months by an FBI agent, George Piro, who speaks Arabic, brings him cookies and cigars, and never raises his voice. Piro is instructed to build rapport, and does. The reports of these sessions are declassified years later and constitute the only extended record of Saddam Hussein speaking without a state around him. He tends a small garden of weeds outside the cell. He asks after his daughters. He explains that he never had the weapons and that he could not say so.
stops.quote: Currently, the only political parties existing in Iraq are the ones with the weapons.
stops.quote_source: FBI Interview Session 1, Baghdad Operations Center, SSA George L. Piro, 7 February 2004, declassified via National Security Archive EBB No. 279
suggested_refs: The FBI interview reports of Saddam Hussein, National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 279
sources: FBI Interview Session 1, 7 February 2004, NSA EBB No. 279

stops.name: Baghdad Green Zone, the first appearance
stops.campa: Brought before an Iraqi investigating judge in a room in the Green Zone, unshackled at the door, he refuses to accept the charges read to him and refuses the court's standing to read them. Asked his name and occupation, he gives his occupation as president of Iraq, present tense. He tells the judge the proceeding is theatre and calls the American president a criminal; the pool reporters in the room record the first phrase as spoken and the second in summary, and no official transcript of the session is ever released.
stops.quote_source: CNN, 'Defiant Saddam rejects court, charges,' 1 July 2004, pool-reporter coverage of the arraignment
suggested_refs: The 1 July 2004 arraignment before the Iraqi Special Tribunal

stops.name: Baghdad Green Zone, the Dujail trial opens
stops.campa: The Iraqi Special Tribunal opens the first case: Saddam Hussein and seven co-defendants, on the one hundred and forty-eight killed at Dujail twenty-three years earlier. He arrives carrying a Quran, argues with the bailiffs about being led by the arm, and refuses to give his name. Over the following year three defence lawyers are murdered and two judges leave the bench. He tells the court his body carries the marks of beatings. The tribunal proceeds. The Anfal case, covering Halabja and the Kurdish campaign, is opened separately and will not be finished.
stops.quote: I do not respond to this so-called court, with all due respect to its people, and I retain my constitutional right as the president of Iraq.
stops.quote_source: Trial of Saddam Hussein, opening session, 19 October 2005, translated court record
suggested_refs: The Dujail trial before the Iraqi Special Tribunal, October 2005 to November 2006

stops.name: Baghdad Green Zone, the sentence
stops.campa: The tribunal convicts him of crimes against humanity in the Dujail case and sentences him to death by hanging. He is ordered to his feet and refuses, and is lifted by the guards. He shouts over the reading of the sentence with his finger in the air, then chants that God is great until he is taken out. The New York Times and the BBC transcribe the shout differently, and the two versions have never been reconciled. On the twenty-sixth of December the appeal court upholds the sentence and orders it carried out within thirty days.
stops.quote: Long live the people! Long live the Arab nation! Down with the spies!
stops.quote_source: Kirk Semple, 'Saddam Hussein Is Sentenced to Death,' New York Times, 5 November 2006
suggested_refs: The Dujail verdict of 5 November 2006 and the appeal ruling of 26 December 2006
sources: Kirk Semple, New York Times, 5 November 2006

stops.name: Camp Justice, Kadhimiya
stops.campa: He is hanged before dawn at Camp Justice, a former military intelligence compound in Kadhimiya, on the first morning of Eid al-Adha. He refuses the hood. The guards on the platform chant the name of Muqtada al-Sadr at him and he answers them, and the exchange is recorded on a mobile phone held up in the room and is on the internet within hours, showing an execution conducted as a sectarian settling of accounts. The official video, silent and edited, is released the same day. Almost nobody watches that one.
stops.quote: I have saved you from destitution and misery and destroyed your enemies, the Persians and Americans.
stops.quote_source: Execution recording and eyewitness accounts, Camp Justice, Baghdad, 30 December 2006, translated
suggested_refs: Camp Justice, Kadhimiya district, Baghdad, site of the execution
sources: Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera reporting, December 2006

stops.name: Al-Awja, the burial before dawn
stops.campa: The body is flown north and buried in al-Awja under twenty-four hours after the drop, before first light, in a tent raised over the ground beside the plot where Uday and Qusay were laid three years earlier. The village he was born in and the village he is buried in are the same village; between the two lies everything. The tent becomes a shrine within months, visited by men of the tribe and by Ba'athists who bring photographs and sit with them, in a country where his name has just been made a criminal thing to say aloud.
suggested_refs: The burial tent at al-Awja and the adjacent graves of Uday and Qusay Hussein

stops.name: Al-Awja, the tomb taken apart
stops.campa: During the fighting for Tikrit the mausoleum at al-Awja is destroyed. One account has Islamic State demolishing it and Shia militiamen afterwards planting their banners in the rubble, one of them Qasem Soleimani's; the Western press of that spring reported the militias burning it themselves. The perpetrator is genuinely contested and is left contested here. A local story, older than the fire, holds that the body in that ground was never his. Whether anything now stands on the site, and where the remains are, this compilation could not establish.
suggested_refs: The Second Battle of Tikrit, March-April 2015, and the destruction of the al-Awja tomb
